blocks.text: In celebration of Criterion’s The Complete Kubrick , we’re publishing a season of features dedicated to the filmmaker’s oeuvre, going through Criterion’s box set era by era and disc by disc—plus a couple of surprises from the archives. Explore more here and read part three below.

In the throes of the 1960 election season, during an interview with Eugene Archer of the New York Times , a 31-year-old Stanley Kubrick defined the protagonists of all his films as “outsiders struggling to do some impossible thing.” To this end, he provocatively likened Kirk Douglas’s tragic anti-establishment heroes in Paths of Glory and Spartacus to the aspiring thieves of The Killing , as well as the already-known character who would become his most challenging and morally compromised lead to date: Humbert Humbert, the silver-tongued literary pedophile of Vladimir Nabokov’s revered and reviled Lolita .

Though shot on less than a sixth of Spartacus ‘ budget and among the visually quietest of Kubrick’s films, Lolita is, in its own way, a work of gobsmacking ambition—or, depending on who you ask, hubris. Even in its time, the idea of filming a recognizable version of Nabokov’s scandalous, prosaically baroque, unreliably narrated first-person novel of sexual immorality—and doing so under the dictates of the Hays Code—was seen as such a madman’s quest that it became the film’s tagline: “ How did they ever make a movie of LOLITA ? ” Nabokov himself—approached by an eager, young Kubrick with a mutual love of chess, boxing, and Russian art, a fawning appreciation for his work, and a generous offer for his participation in the film—expressed public skepticism. Yet Nabokov also gave Kubrick his blessing and contributed the foundational draft of the screenplay, for which he retained sole, Oscar-nominated credit despite multiple redrafts by Kubrick and several ghostwriters without the original author’s input. (A novice screenwriter for all his mastery of fiction, Nabokov’s submitted draft was of doorstopper width more appropriate to a miniseries than feature, while Kubrick would say privately of its contents that Nabokov was “a literary genius…[who] can’t write a line of dialogue.”)

Guided by Nabokov’s suggestions, however, the film does manage a surprisingly compelling answer to its inquisitive tagline. Where Humbert’s gilded narration makes the novel an intimate character study of a romantic monster, Kubrick’s largely plot-faithful film subtly reframes its story as the comedy of a cowardly predator whose maniacal fears and fantasies seem to manifest into a subtly heightened reality. James Mason (a one-time star for Kubrick hero Max Ophüls) plays Humbert just shy of Looney Tunes for the New Yorker set, a comically impotent image of fallen Continental sophistication: a bathrobe-loving European poet with a voice like slightly overripe olive oil, beset on all sides by vulgar Americans, cringing and slinking around worshipful midcult consumers and desperate housewives of the New Hampshire suburbs, pursuing the elusive underage girl of his dreams with a verbose, withering, wounded neuroticism. The image of Mason’s shrinking frame and sweating visage juxtaposed with the sly, sonorous erudition of his internal monologue is a barbed bonbon of cinematic irony that’s more than enough to justify even a flawed movie of Lolita , though Kubrick curiously underutilizes it. Seemingly too afraid of relying on voiceover, the film excludes all but a few brief samples of Humbert’s inner articulation, despite working from some of the tastiest inner-monologuing in English literature.

In its biggest change from the novel, though, Lolita ‘s unique framing device—a Citizen Kane and Sunset Boulevard -inspired noirish in medias res start wherein death visits a dilapidated culturati’s mansion—refocuses the largely plot-faithful adaptation’s story around a duel of pedophile sophisticates between Humbert and his wilier American counterpart, Clare Quilty. Greatly expanding Quilty’s role from the novel, the film becomes an absurd, one-sided two-hander in which Mason’s Humbert, busy stewing in his own sick, overeducated head, is repeatedly teased, tortured, and hoodwinked by a girl-snatching, show-stealing master of disguise and new Kubrick fascination: Peter Sellers. Not for the first time working with Kubrick, Sellers would be a crucial tool in drawing out the latent satiric venom of the source material. Appearing as a celebrity TV writer with premonitions of Woody Allen (another Kubrick fascination), a stuttering detective, a slick-haired German psychologist, a disembodied voice on the phone, and eventually a partied-out libertine past his prime, Sellers’ slithering, seemingly servile Quilty continually undercuts and out-molests the more intellectual, introspective, comically gullible Humbert—and, implicitly, the American public—with fast-talking caricatures of respectable authority figures, directly anticipating the multi-faced geopolitical buffoonery of his three roles in Dr. Strangelove . Kubrick, obsessed with literal and figurative masks, was enamored with the blankness and malleability of Sellers’s mercurial funny-man persona, and deploys it to appropriately ticklish and unsettling effect in Lolita as his all-surface acting style clashes with Mason’s to the point of seeming to have walked in from a different movie. That’s the idea, of course, as Sellers conveys the facile genius of the all-American con man overtaking the weary, navel-gazing European on the midcentury battlefields of art, governance, the life of the mind, and the predatory seduction of their mutual object of desire: the blonde-haired, blue-eyed girl willfully oblivious to the lofty heights of culture and the depressing complexities of adulthood.

Or is she? Sue Lyon, 14 at the time of shooting but expressly cast for physical maturity relative to her age, embodies a Dolores Haze positioned by Kubrick as a provocative enigma. In Humbert’s fevered vision, she’s somehow at once a helpless innocent and winking seductress wielding arcane power over him. Kubrick and Lyon prod audience comfort zones by creating an uncannily precocious character whose affected girlish mannerisms—her alternating approach and resistance to the obsessed and emasculated Humbert, her mascara-wearing, lollipop-sucking, poster-making gaze over the rims of her heart-shaped sunglasses—could be read either way, as Humbert first waits to have his way with her and then, by the end, she has her way with him. Even while he kidnaps and abuses her (offscreen), the “innocent” Lolita seems to have his whole number, more than enough to effectively squeeze and dupe him in the long con, to her questionable benefit. Their queasy balance of power is visualized in the most explicit image the film can get away with: a fawning, kneeling Humbert stroking and manicuring the toes of “his” Lolita as the girl lies back with candy and teen-fashion magazines like a middle-school Cleopatra. As Psychologist Quilty babbles in his mock-German patois before Humbert’s sweaty grip on his illicit daughter-lover begins to slip in the film’s final act: “She eizer has exceptional control, or she has no control at all. Ve cannot decide vhich!”

Dolores’s desperate situation—a life of domestic misery with a potential escape ticket in the pocket of an exotic man of means—is both reinforced by and darkly mirrored in the toxic, tragic presence of Shelley Winters as her onetime-teen-bride single mother, Charlotte. Winters, who reportedly infuriated Kubrick on set by repeatedly failing to memorize her lines yet whom he refused to fire, spends every other scene on the verge of hysterical tears as the bitterly ironic film’s thorny hidden heart: where the leggy daughter she openly resents is an alluring bundle of unknown potential, Charlotte is currency already spent in the erotic economy that lusts after Lolitas. Trying to claw back any sense of self-ownership and status from a “normalcy”-fixated suburban world that regards her advancing age and lack of a husband with chilly secondhand embarrassment, the progressively unraveling Winters plays a wine-guzzling, cringe-inducing, miserably lonely Cluster B tyrant who clings, moans, emotionally saps, and crudely manipulates the other begrudging members of her dysfunctional household, even while the comically cowering Humbert manipulates her in turn for access to her rebellious daughter. Crucially, Winters and Kubrick leave ambiguous just how conscious the seemingly oblivious Charlotte is of her fancy new husband’s unwholesome intentions; she leverages them, for a time, to her attention-seeking benefit. (Kubrick and producer James P. Harris would later recall, with evident unease, the overwhelming volume of mothers who wrote in to Harris-Kubrick Pictures during the casting of Lolita to volunteer their barely pubescent daughters for the part of the titular “nymphet.”)

Winters’s pretentiously dimwitted Charlotte, with hints of arrested development in her nakedly emotive voice and elephantine physicality—her garish wardrobe and confident mangling of foreign words—walks the knife’s edge of contemptible and piteous as she helps lay the groundwork to mold her daughter into an echo of herself and her pain. Kubrick reminds the audience of that pain in eerily lingering shots of Charlotte’s sobbing, room-trashing breakdowns at the peaks of her ruinous fear of abandonment, always just after we’ve been casually invited to despise and laugh at her. When not entertaining the comic urbanity and ironic detachment of its self-pitying predator, the film periodically snaps the audience back to reality and moral common sense with the briefest of gazes into the scared, distant eyes of Humbert’s victims when they aren’t performing for him.

Winters’ wincing tragicomic performance ends up so much the unsung linchpin of Kubrick’s rendition, in fact, that the film loses much of its punch and momentum after she exits partway through. The latter half increasingly struggles to play nice with the source text as it condenses time, scope, and unfilmable episodes from the more loosely structured corresponding portions of the novel into only the key plot events and creeping approach of Sellers, with the actual pedophilia wrestled to the level of subtext. With Lyon remaining on the periphery—partly for artistic reasons, partly for censorship-necessitated ones—Kubrick’s vision of his self-described “bizarre love story” ultimately hinges on how much sympathy one can muster for Mason’s pathetic Humbert as his romantic self-mythology crashes down around him.

Both Kubrick and Nabokov would later lament, without fully disowning the film, that it is a compromised work and likely could not have been any other way. It bears the distinction among Kubrick’s filmography of being the only literary adaptation whose cultural impact remains fully eclipsed by that of its source text, and like Nabokov’s at times alarmingly appropriated novel, Lolita casts its own dark shadow outside the world of fiction. Rumors persist that Lyon, who won a Golden Globe for the role, was herself groomed and abused during production—without Kubrick’s participation or knowledge—and while she never made any specific allegations prior to her death in 2019, she did express bitterness about the role and particular kind of attention it brought into her young life. Two years before Lyon—by then long retired from acting and the public eye, following a string of failed marriages and mental-health crises—credited Lolita with her “destruction as a person,” an 11-year-old Natalie Portman’s tacitly eroticized breakout role in Léon: The Professional made her the “Lolita-like” starlet of a new generation. Portman’s publicly aired misgivings about that role decades later, in a post-#MeToo Hollywood, rhyme uncomfortably with Lyon’s.

Despite its troubled legacy, Kubrick’s Lolita retains a core of admirers. In its time, Kubrick skeptics Pauline Kael and Jean-Luc Godard (who, since razzing The Killing in the pages of Cahiers du cinéma , had become a filmmaker of some reputation himself) uncharacteristically praised Kubrick’s pitch-black comedy and restrained evocations of sin, delusion, and desperation in the margins of Americana. Sofia Coppola names it her favorite Kubrick film, as does the late David Lynch, who dubbed it a work about “time in America” that, like his own, “captures hidden things” about the suburbs. As what could reasonably be considered the final entry in Kubrick’s early Hollywood period—and the first one shot almost entirely in London— Lolita is also rife with the DNA of his subsequent projects without being overly similar to any of them. Its explorations of taboo sexuality, domestic subterfuge, the pursuit of control, and social class as moral and sexual bargaining chips keenly predict Eyes Wide Shut , and its loquaciously vile literary antihero sets the stage for the more demonically energetic punk aesthete of A Clockwork Orange . Most obviously, Lolita ‘s irony-soaked comic castration of the unspeakable and Nabokov-assisted facility for ticklishly ribald, Mad Magazine -adjacent naming conventions—Humbert picks up Dolores from “Camp Climax for Girls” to drive to a hotel staffed by names like “Mr. Swine” and “Mr. Putz”—combine with the many-faced trickery of Peter Sellers to put the key assets in play for the creative breakthrough of Kubrick’s very next film, arguably his first true masterpiece.
